title: Word and body (Dei Verbum 21)
hook: the Church venerates scripture as she venerates the Lord's body
tomorrow: can one place be both the mountaintop and the spring?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dei Verbum 2: God speaks as to friends, and both plain words and shared ones can answer. The line was as friends.

People kiss what they love: a wedding ring, an old photo, the top of a child's head. At Mass, after the Gospel is read, the priest or deacon bends and kisses the page. A few minutes later, the same hands lift the host. Two gestures of honor, one for a book and one for bread. Dei Verbum 21 sets those two side by side, on purpose.
screen: `PEOPLE KISS WHAT THEY LOVE.` → `A KISS FOR THE PAGE.` → `THE SAME HANDS LIFT THE HOST.`

segments.voice: First, the bold sentence. The council says the Church has always venerated the divine scriptures just as she venerates the body of the Lord. That's a strong comparison from a Church that kneels before the Eucharist. It doesn't say the book is the sacrament. It says the honor runs in the same direction. Second, the table. Especially in the liturgy, the paragraph says, the Church receives and offers the bread of life from one table, the table of the word of God and of the body of Christ. One table, two courses. The readings aren't a warm-up before the real thing; they're served from the same place. Third, the meeting. In the sacred books, Dei Verbum says, the Father in heaven comes lovingly to meet his children and talks with them. That picks up yesterday's friendship: the page is where the conversation keeps happening. Fourth, the food. The paragraph calls the word of God support and energy for the Church, food for the soul, a pure and lasting source of spiritual life. One to tell a friend: as he kisses the book, the Roman Missal has the priest say a short prayer under his breath, that through the Gospel's words our sins be wiped away. Word and body, honored together.
screen: `HONORED LIKE THE LORD'S BODY.` · `ONE TABLE, TWO COURSES.` · `THE FATHER MEETS HIS CHILDREN.` · `FOOD FOR THE SOUL.` · then, large: `WORD AND BODY.`

segments.voice: If there's a Bible nearby, hold it in both hands and feel its weight for a few breaths, then open it anywhere and read one verse slowly. If you pray, you can kiss the page or trace a small cross on it, as is done at Mass. If no Bible is near, rest your open hands on your knees and let the quiet be the table.
Word and body. Dei Verbum 21's pairing: scripture and the Eucharist, served from one table and honored together. Today's word.
Your line: word and body. The readings come from the same table as the bread. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At Mass, the priest or deacon who proclaims the Gospel kisses the book afterward, saying a short prayer quietly, and in many churches the Book of the Gospels is carried in procession and placed on the altar.

chat.says: baccalaureate mass tomorrow and they asked me to do the first reading. it's just reading out loud, right?
options: Not just. The council honors the word like the Lord's body. Read it like serving bread.
Pretty much. The readings warm people up; communion is the real part of Mass.
Right. Only the priest's Gospel counts, so the first reading barely matters.
chat.meaning: Dei Verbum 21 says the Church venerates scripture as she venerates the Lord's body, offering the bread of life from one table.

Dei Verbum.meaning: Vatican II's constitution on God's word; Latin for the word of God

Eucharist.meaning: the bread and wine of Mass, for Catholics the body and blood of Christ

host.meaning: the round wafer of bread consecrated at Mass

deacon.meaning: an ordained minister who proclaims the Gospel and serves

Roman Missal.meaning: the book of prayers and directions for celebrating Mass

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation

notes: Dei Verbum 21 paraphrased (official English not public domain): confirm 'always venerated the divine scriptures just as she venerates the body of the Lord', 'one table of the word of God and of the body of Christ', 'the Father meets his children with great love and speaks with them', 'support and energy', 'food of the soul', 'pure and lasting source of spiritual life'.
'Always' is the council's own word in DV 21, not the script's claim.

The kiss of the Gospel book and its quiet prayer ('Per evangelica dicta deleantur nostra delicta': through the words of the Gospel may our sins be wiped away): confirm against GIRM 134 and the Order of Mass. The deacon says the same prayer when he proclaims the Gospel; the voice says 'the priest' for simplicity.
Practice suggests kissing the page or signing it 'if you pray'; confirm this is a fitting invitation for private reading.
Original game: 'mensa' as in DV 21's Latin (ex mensa tam verbi Dei quam Corporis Christi); confirm with a Latinist.
v3 senses shape: a kiss, the book's weight in the hands, and bread carry the idea; the practice is physical.
